name: David Crockett State Park
cost: Free, camping and canoe rental extra
unique: A park on Shoal Creek at the site of the powder mill and gristmill Crockett ran before he went to Congress, with a lake, a swimming pool, trails to the mill race and campgrounds under the hardwoods.
buzz: The creek and the lake are the reasons locals go, and the mill story is the reason to read the signs. It is a working family park rather than a monument.

name: James D. Vaughan Gospel Music Museum
customer: Gospel music fans, church groups, historians
unique: A museum to the man who started the first professional Southern gospel quartet, founded a publishing house and a radio station, and made Lawrenceburg the center of the genre, with sheet music, recordings, robes and the original recording equipment.
buzz: Church groups come by the busload and the volunteers know the catalogue by heart. Visitors are surprised that a whole American music business started in a small Tennessee town.

name: Amish Community at Ethridge
cost: Free to drive, goods priced per item
dates: Year round, closed Sundays; best Thursday to Saturday
customer: Food shoppers, bakers, back road drivers
unique: A working Amish settlement strung along straight farm roads, with bulk food stores, a bakery, a harness shop, greenhouses and produce stands, where the fields are worked with horses and the buggies share the road.
buzz: People drive from Nashville for the bulk foods and the cinnamon rolls. Etiquette matters here: no photographs of people, no Sunday visiting, and cash is expected.

name: Lawrenceburg Public Square
unique: A courthouse square with a 1900s courthouse in the middle and a ring of brick storefronts, in the town where Crockett lived, the gospel music business started and the Trail of Tears crossed Shoal Creek.
buzz: Small and busy enough to feel alive on a weekday. The square is the place to eat before driving out to Ethridge or the park.

name: Milky Way Farm
customer: Architecture fans, candy history people, event shoppers
unique: The 1930s estate of Frank Mars, the candy bar inventor, with a twenty five thousand square foot manor, a chandelier barn, stone outbuildings and acres of rolling Giles County pasture that used to be a showplace horse farm.
buzz: Tours are by reservation and the house is the draw, with the candy fortune story told room by room. People who expect a factory are surprised it is a country estate instead.

name: Historic Downtown Pulaski
company: Visit Pulaski and the City of Pulaski
unique: A courthouse square of 1800s commercial buildings around a 1909 courthouse, in a town with a complicated history that includes both a Civil War hospital story and the 1860s founding of the Ku Klux Klan a few blocks away, which the county's own history markers confront rather than hide.
buzz: The square is well kept and the shops are local. People come for the architecture and the Sam Davis story and leave talking about how the town handles the harder part of its past.

name: Elk River at Elkton
unique: A slow, gravel bottomed river with a public access at the Matt Gardner area, where the water is shallow enough to wade, the smallmouth bite in summer and the shoals are the only thing between you and the next county.
buzz: Anglers float it for smallmouth and locals swim the holes in July. It is a working river rather than a park, so bring what you need.

name: Prichard's Distillery
unique: A whiskey distillery in a 1920s schoolhouse in a town of a hundred people, making rum and Tennessee whiskey in copper pot stills small enough that the tour is a walk around the room and the smell is the main exhibit.
buzz: The tasting is generous and the rum is the surprise for people who came for whiskey. Tour groups are small and the guides answer questions about the still rather than reciting a script.

name: Fayetteville Square and Antique District
unique: A courthouse square and surrounding blocks that have become one of the region's antique destinations, with dealers in old storefronts selling furniture, glass, tools and the estate contents of middle Tennessee.
buzz: Dealers say the buyers come from Huntsville and Nashville. The square is walkable and the prices are better than the city, which is the whole reason for the drive.

name: Stone Bridge Park
unique: A memorial park beside the Elk River built around the stone bridge that carried the road into town, with a paved walk, a fishing bank, a visitor center and the kind of shade that makes a July afternoon bearable.
buzz: It is where Fayetteville walks its dogs and eats lunch. The bridge is the landmark and the river below it is shallow and clear.

name: Henry Horton State Park
unique: Fifteen hundred acres on the Duck River built on the old governor's farm, with a lodge, cabins, an eighteen hole golf course, a swimming pool, a trap range and river frontage where the water is clear enough to see the bottom.
buzz: The golf course and the pool make it a family weekend, and the Duck River is why paddlers come. People who grew up going there bring their own children.

name: Duck River Float
dates: April to October, water level dependent
company: Local outfitters at Henry Horton and around Columbia
unique: A float on what biologists call the most biologically diverse river of its size in North America, with more than a hundred species of fish and mussels under a canoe that draws six inches of water.
buzz: Outfitters run shuttles from the park and the river is easy enough for children. People talk about the mussel beds and the number of turtles on the logs.

name: Lewisburg Square and Dixie Theatre
dates: Year round; theater on show nights
company: City of Lewisburg and Marshall County Community Theater
unique: A courthouse square with a 1920s theater still used by the community theater company, surrounded by locally owned shops in a town that has held onto its downtown while the interstate grew around it.
buzz: The Dixie is the reason to check the calendar, and the square is a good walk on a Saturday. Locals describe the town as small but not sleepy.

name: President James K. Polk Home and Museum
company: President James K. Polk Memorial Association
unique: The only home of the eleventh president that survives, a brick Federal house his father built, with original family furniture, the White House china and a museum that takes the Mexican War and the Oregon boundary seriously rather than as a footnote.
buzz: Docents give the tour and are honest about the expansionist record. People working through all the presidential sites call it one of the better small ones.

name: Elm Springs
customer: Architecture fans, history travellers, event planners
unique: An 1837 Greek Revival mansion by the master builder Nathan Vaught, with a curving staircase, original outbuildings and a history that runs from a plantation economy through a Union occupation to a twentieth century restoration.
buzz: The woodwork and the staircase are what people photograph. Tours are small and the guides know the family and the enslaved labor records.

name: Rippavilla
customer: Civil War travellers, architecture fans, families
unique: A hundred acre antebellum farm with a restored 1855 house that sat between the armies during the 1864 Franklin and Spring Hill fighting, with guided tours that cover the family, the enslaved workers and the battle that came to the front yard.
buzz: The house is beautiful and the tour does not skip the difficult parts. People pair it with the Carter House and Carnton for a full day of the Franklin campaign.

name: Columbia Square and Muletown
unique: A wide courthouse square with a fountain, ghost signs on the brick, a bronze mule in honor of the town's nickname and a surrounding district of shops, bakeries and a listening room in a converted building.
buzz: The square has become a Nashville day trip for people who want a smaller version of it. The mule statue is the meeting point and the concert series fills the lawn in summer.

name: Buffalo River Canoe Float
unique: A national scenic river with bluffs, gravel bars and no development, floated in canoes rented from a family that has run the same stretch since 1991, with camping at the put in and a shuttle that takes the logistics away.
buzz: People float it every summer and describe the water as the clearest in middle Tennessee. Weekdays are empty and the rope swing at the halfway sandbar is the traditional stop.

name: Natchez Trace Parkway in Wayne County
unique: A two lane parkway with no trucks and no billboards, following the old Chickasaw and Kaintuck trace across the ridges, with pullouts at the graves, the old stands and the sections where the sunken path is still visible in the woods.
buzz: Cyclists ride it for the traffic free miles and drivers stop at every pullout because there is nothing else to do and that is the point. Spring and fall are the seasons.

name: Waynesboro Courthouse Square
unique: A small square with a 1900s courthouse, a monument and a row of stores in a county that has been logging, farming and floating the Buffalo for two centuries.
buzz: It is a fifteen minute walk and the place to buy ice before the river. Locals wave at strangers, which visitors notice.

name: Meriwether Lewis Monument and Grave
company: National Park Service, Natchez Trace Parkway
unique: The broken column over the grave of the explorer who died on this stretch of the trace in 1809 at thirty five, in a clearing with a pioneer cemetery, a cabin site and the old trace path running into the trees.
buzz: The broken column is deliberate, and the rangers tell the story of the death and the disputed accounts without pretending to settle them. People stop for fifteen minutes and stay an hour.

name: Fall Hollow Falls
company: National Park Service, Natchez Trace Parkway
unique: A boardwalk and a short trail down into a hollow where two small creeks drop over the sandstone, one falling in front of you and one behind, right off the parkway at milepost 391.9.
buzz: The easiest waterfall stop on the trace and most people have it to themselves. It is a ten minute walk and the boardwalk makes it accessible.

name: Lewis County Museum of Natural History
unique: A county museum with two halves: the local history of a county carved out of the trace country, and the Maddox wildlife collection, a room of mounted birds and mammals from the surrounding hills.
buzz: Small and free, and the wildlife room is what children remember. Volunteers are glad to have visitors and will tell you where the good gravel roads go.

name: Mousetail Landing State Park
unique: Thirteen hundred acres on the east bank of the Tennessee River, with a campground, a swimming pool, a boat ramp and a trail along the bluffs where the river is wide and the current is slow.
buzz: It is a locals' park with a river view and cheap camping. Boaters use it as a base for the river and the fall colors on the bluffs are the quiet season.

name: Commodore Hotel and Cafe
customer: Couples, river trippers, small town travellers
unique: A 1939 hotel on Linden's main street, rescued from ruin in 2007 and restored room by room, with a cafe downstairs, a porch over the square and rates that assume you are passing through rather than on business.
buzz: Guests talk about the porch and the breakfast. It is the reason people stop in Linden instead of driving on, and the town has built a small tourism economy around it.

name: Linden Courthouse Square
unique: A 1920s courthouse square with a restored main street, a 1940s gas station and shops in a town of a thousand people on the Buffalo River road.
buzz: Small enough that people notice a new face. The square is the model for what a town can do with a hotel and a main street.

name: Grinder's Switch and the Minnie Pearl Story
customer: Comedy and country music fans, roadside hunters
unique: The railroad switch outside Centerville that Sarah Ophelia Colley Cannon turned into a fictional hometown for Minnie Pearl, complete with a country road sign, a small exhibit in the chamber office and the hat with the price tag still on it.
buzz: Fans of the Grand Ole Opry make the drive and are delighted that the switch is really just a switch. The chamber volunteers tell the story better than any museum label.

name: Duck River at Centerville
unique: A stretch of the Duck through Hickman County where the river runs clear over gravel, the mussel beds are intact and the access points are a few miles apart, which makes it the quiet float in the region.
buzz: Locals float it in summer and anglers work the shoals for bass and catfish. It is not the managed park experience, so bring two cars and a map.

name: Centerville Courthouse Square
unique: A square with a 1900s courthouse and a ring of brick storefronts in the only incorporated town in Hickman County, where the county fair and the Minnie Pearl festival both have their parade.
buzz: The square is small and the county is proud of it. People stop on the way to the river and end up staying for lunch.
